THOUGHT: This 17-year-old male presents with a classic triad of symptoms highly suggestive of reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter’s syndrome): (1) asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis (right knee swelling/pain, prior left ankle involvement), (2) urethritis (dysuria for 3 weeks, with pyuria on urinalysis — WBC 12–16/hpf — in the absence of urinary tract infection signs like bacteriuria or systemic toxicity), and (3) conjunctivitis (bilateral conjunctival inflammation). Additional supportive features include enthesitis (tenderness at left Achilles insertion), low-grade fever (38°C), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 38 mm/h, leukocytosis 12,300/mm³), and synovial fluid analysis showing inflammatory arthritis (26,000 WBC/mm³, 75% neutrophils, cloudy appearance, negative Gram stain — ruling out septic arthritis as primary cause). His sexual history (multiple partners, inconsistent condom use) raises concern for a preceding Chlamydia trachomatis infection — the most common trigger of reactive arthritis in young sexually active individuals in developed countries. While HIV was tested and negative, other STIs (e.g., chlamydia, gonorrhea) remain untested but clinically highly relevant. The absence of rheumatoid factor, young age, lack of symmetric small-joint involvement, and family history of RA (which is not associated with reactive arthritis) make RA unlikely. Gout or pseudogout are improbable given age, absence of tophi or crystal analysis, and clinical context. Septic arthritis is less likely due to negative Gram stain, absence of systemic toxicity (normal HR, BP), and the presence of extra-articular features (conjunctivitis, urethritis, enthesitis) pointing to a systemic reactive process. The constellation — arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis + enthesitis + HLA-B27–associated pattern (though not tested) — fulfills diagnostic criteria for reactive arthritis.

DIAGNOSIS: Reactive arthritis
